vignette: A man has lost vibration sense and joint position sense in his right leg and foot. Pain and temperature sensation are normal. Strength is normal.
prompt: Where is the lesion?
answer: Right dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis) of the spinal cord, ipsilateral, below the sensory decussation

vignette: A patient cannot feel pinprick or hot/cold on the left leg and trunk below the umbilicus. Vibration and strength are intact on both sides.
prompt: Which tract is damaged, and on which side?
answer: Right anterolateral (spinothalamic) tract, contralateral to the deficit, a segment or two above the level of loss

vignette: A patient has an uncoordinated gait with poor limb position awareness in the left leg, without weakness and without loss of pain sense.
prompt: Which spinal pathway is most likely damaged?
answer: Left dorsal spinocerebellar tract (unconscious proprioception), ipsilateral
review_note: Vignette synthesised from lecture 5 pathway content; no direct course vignette.

vignette: After a stroke a patient has a stiff, weak right arm and leg with brisk reflexes and an upgoing great toe on plantar stimulation.
prompt: Is this an upper or lower motor neuron lesion, and what is the paralysis called?
answer: Upper motor neuron lesion: spastic paralysis

vignette: A patient has a floppy, wasted right forearm with absent reflexes and fasciculations after a nerve injury.
prompt: Is this an upper or lower motor neuron lesion, and what is the paralysis called?
answer: Lower motor neuron lesion: flaccid paralysis with atrophy

vignette: A stab wound hemisects the right side of the spinal cord at T10. Examine the patient below the level of the lesion.
prompt: Describe the deficits on each side.
answer: Right: spastic weakness and loss of vibration/proprioception (ipsilateral); left: loss of pain and temperature (contralateral)
review_note: Not in the course slides (standard neuroanatomy); TA owner to confirm it is in scope. Derived from lecture 5/10 tract positions.

vignette: A man develops sudden paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensation below T8 on both sides, but vibration sense and proprioception are preserved.
prompt: Which vessel is occluded, and why is the dorsal column spared?
answer: Anterior spinal artery; the dorsal columns are supplied by the two posterior spinal arteries

vignette: A patient has bilateral loss of vibration and position sense with preserved strength and pain sensation after surgery.
prompt: Which arteries are most likely compromised?
answer: Posterior spinal arteries (supply the dorsal columns and part of the dorsal horns)

vignette: A patient with a cervical cord lesion at C8-T1 has ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
prompt: Which cell group is interrupted?
answer: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons of the lateral (intermediolateral) horn / descending sympathetic fibers (Horner syndrome)
review_note: Not in the course slides (standard neuroanatomy); TA owner to confirm it is in scope.

vignette: A patient has low back pain, saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention with flaccid leg weakness.
prompt: Which structure is compressed?
answer: Cauda equina (lumbosacral roots below the conus medullaris): a lower motor neuron picture

vignette: A needle is placed between L3 and L4 to sample CSF.
prompt: Why is this level considered safe?
answer: The adult spinal cord ends at L1/L2 (conus medullaris); below it only the cauda equina floats in the lumbar cistern

vignette: A patient with a dorsal root lesion has numbness over a strip of skin of the thigh.
prompt: What is the name of the skin territory supplied by a single spinal nerve root?
answer: Dermatome

vignette: A man with a cardiac event feels pain in the left arm. Another patient with diaphragm irritation feels pain at the tip of the shoulder.
prompt: Why does diaphragm irritation refer to the shoulder?
answer: The diaphragm is innervated by C3-C5 (phrenic nerve), the same dermatomes as the shoulder; dorsal horn neurons receive both inputs

vignette: A fracture through the cribriform plate of the anterior cranial fossa follows a car crash.
prompt: Which sense is lost and which cranial nerve is damaged?
answer: Smell (anosmia), olfactory nerve (CN I)

vignette: A patient understands speech but speaks in effortful, halting phrases of few words. Repetition is impaired.
prompt: Which cortical area is damaged and what is the aphasia called?
answer: Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus, left); Broca's (expressive) aphasia

vignette: A patient speaks fluently but with meaningless words and cannot understand spoken commands.
prompt: Which area is damaged and what is the aphasia called?
answer: Wernicke's area (posterior superior temporal gyrus, left); Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia

vignette: A patient with a right parietal lesion ignores the left side of space, does not dress the left side and misses food on the left of her plate.
prompt: What syndrome is this?
answer: Hemineglect syndrome (contralateral neglect from non-dominant, right parietal damage)

vignette: A stroke damages the left transverse temporal gyrus (Heschl's gyrus).
prompt: What deficit would result?
answer: Impaired hearing (primary auditory cortex), mostly in the contralateral ear

vignette: A tumour compresses the medial surface of the right precentral gyrus.
prompt: Which body part is weak, and on which side?
answer: Left leg and foot (medial motor homunculus; contralateral)

vignette: A patient has loss of the left half of the visual field in both eyes after a stroke.
prompt: Which region of cortex is damaged?
answer: Right primary visual cortex (calcarine fissure region)

vignette: A patient with a lesion near the insula loses awareness of her heartbeat and stomach sensations.
prompt: Which cortical area maps emotions and visceral feelings onto the body?
answer: Insular cortex

vignette: A patient after a frontal injury shows apathy and cannot initiate goal-directed behavior.
prompt: Which region is most likely damaged?
answer: Anterior cingulate cortex (motivation)

vignette: A tumour blocks both foramina of Monro.
prompt: Which structures enlarge?
answer: The lateral ventricles (obstructive hydrocephalus); the third and fourth ventricles do not

vignette: A child has an enlarged head and dilated lateral and third ventricles, but a normal fourth ventricle.
prompt: Where is the obstruction?
answer: Cerebral aqueduct (aqueductal stenosis)
review_note: Synthesised from ventricular anatomy (lecture 2); no direct vignette in the course.

vignette: Low maternal folate in early pregnancy raises the risk of which malformations?
prompt: Name the group of defects.
answer: Neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly)
